User: I want to file my 2024 taxes correctly. I'm single in Austin TX. W-2 from Pacific Software: $96,500. Additional income: $18,400 (freelance writing, 5 clients), $2,100 from Capital One 360, $420 from Schwab. Home office: 120 sq ft exclusive; I pay $1,750/month for 720 sq ft. Deductions: $3,200 student loan interest (Nelnet, 2018–2021); $1,500 to Salvation Army have the receipt; $540 unreimbursed expenses. Can you tell me what I can deduct, whether to itemize or take the standard deduction, how to treat the home office, and what forms I need?
Assistant: Thanks — that’s a good, complete set of numbers. Below I’ll (A) summarize what’s deductible, (B) compare itemizing vs. the standard deduction, (C) explain treatment of the home office and which method is likely best for you, (D) list the forms you’ll need, and (E) give next steps and a few clarifying questions. I’ll also mark items where eligibility depends on income limits or on whether an expense is business vs. employee-related.

Short disclaimer: I’m not a CPA — for complex situations or to be certain about phaseouts, please consider a tax preparer or CPA. I’ll use IRS rules in effect through mid‑2024.

A. What you can deduct (summary)
- Self-employment business expenses (Schedule C)
  - Your freelance writing income ($18,400) is reported on Schedule C. You may deduct ordinary & necessary business expenses on Schedule C. That includes either:
    - Home office allocation of rent/utilities (actual-expense method), or
    - The simplified home‑office method ($5/sq ft up to 300 sq ft).
  - If the $540 “unreimbursed expenses” were for your freelance work, they are deductible on Schedule C. If they were unreimbursed employee expenses from a W-2 job, they are NOT deductible for 2018–2025 (suspended by TCJA).
- Self-employment tax deduction
  - You must pay self-employment (SE) tax on net self-employment income; half of the SE tax is an above‑the‑line deduction on Form 1040 (reported on Schedule 1).
- Interest income
  - Interest from Capital One 360 ($2,100) and Schwab ($420) — total $2,520 — is taxable interest income. Because your taxable interest > $1,500, you’ll also use Schedule B (Interest and Ordinary Dividends).
- Student loan interest
  - The student loan interest deduction (maximum $2,500) is an above‑the‑line deduction IF you meet the MAGI limits. Given the income you reported, you are likely over the phaseout and therefore probably NOT eligible. (You paid $3,200 in interest, but the statutory maximum is $2,500 and the deduction phases out for higher MAGI.)
- Charitable gifts
  - Cash gift of $1,500 to Salvation Army is an itemized deduction (Schedule A) only if you itemize. If you take the standard deduction, you cannot separately deduct it on your 1040 (unless special temporary rules apply, which do not generally apply in 2024).

B. Itemize vs. standard deduction — which is likely better for you
- The standard deduction for single filers is larger than your likely itemized deductions here. You only listed $1,500 in charitable gifts and no mortgage interest, state income tax (you live in Texas), or large medical expenses. So your itemized total will be roughly $1,500 — well below the standard deduction.
- Conclusion: Take the standard deduction. (Itemizing would only make sense if you have other deductible items not listed — significant mortgage interest, real property taxes, large medical expenses, or additional charitable gifts.)

C. Home office: actual vs. simplified method and how it affects your tax picture
You said: home is 720 sq ft, home office exclusively used is 120 sq ft.
- Home-office percentage = 120 / 720 = 16.666...% (≈16.67%).

Two methods:
1) Simplified method
  - $5 per sq ft × 120 sq ft = $600 deduction (no Form 8829). Simple, but often smaller for renters with significant rent.
2) Actual-expense method
  - Allocate a share of actual home expenses to the business. For rent: $1,750/mo × 12 = $21,000 annual rent × 16.67% = $3,500 rent portion deductible on Schedule C.
  - You can also allocate a share of utilities, renter’s insurance, etc., if you pay them. (If you own, depreciation and mortgage interest rules also come into play.)
  - Because you are renting and rent is large, the actual method will likely produce a much larger deduction (~$3,500 just from rent) than the simplified $600.
- How to report
  - For an actual-method home-office deduction, you normally use Form 8829 (Expenses for Business Use of Your Home) and transfer the allowable deduction to your Schedule C.
  - If you use the simplified method, compute it and report it on Schedule C (no Form 8829).
- Important requirement: the space must be used exclusively and regularly for your business, and it must be your principal place of business (or used to meet clients, etc.). You said it is exclusive 120 sq ft — that supports eligibility.

D. Forms you’ll need (typical list for your situation)
- Form 1040 (federal individual income tax return).
- Attach your W-2 from Pacific Software (wages $96,500).
- Schedule 1 (Form 1040): additional income and adjustments (self-employment income flows through Schedule C, adjustments like the deductible part of self‑employment tax and possibly student-loan interest go here).
- Schedule C (Form 1040): report freelance income ($18,400) and business expenses, including home-office deduction (unless using simplified method).
- Form 8829: use this ONLY if you choose the actual-expense method for the home office.
- Schedule SE (Form 1040): compute self-employment tax on net self-employment income. Half of SE tax is deductible (reported on Schedule 1).
- Schedule B (Form 1040): required since taxable interest ($2,520) > $1,500.
- Form 8995 (or 8995-A) — Qualified Business Income (QBI) deduction: if eligible, you may be able to take up to 20% of qualified business income from your Schedule C. Whether you can claim QBI and how much depends on taxable income thresholds and the nature of the business. You might be eligible — run the numbers (tax prep software or CPA will compute this for you automatically).
- Keep any 1099-NEC, 1099-MISC, 1099-INT, and your receipts, and attach or input them to your return as required.

E. Rough numerical impacts (estimates)
(These are illustrative; exact numbers change with other expenses or tax-year inflation adjustments.)

Option A — Actual home office used for calculation:
- Schedule C gross income: $18,400
- Less home office rent allocation: −$3,500 → net Schedule C profit = $14,900
- Net earnings subject to SE tax = 14,900 × 92.35% = ≈ $13,761
- SE tax ≈ 13,761 × 15.3% ≈ $2,106. (You’ll pay about $2,106 in SE tax.)
- Deductible half of SE tax ≈ $1,053 (above the line).
- AGI roughly: wages 96,500 + interest 2,520 + net business profit 14,900 = 113,920 → minus half SE tax 1,053 → AGI ≈ $112,867.
- Student loan interest phaseout: with AGI around $112k, you’re likely over the phaseout limit for the student loan interest deduction (so probably ineligible).

Option B — Simplified home-office method:
- Home-office deduction = $600, so Schedule C profit = 18,400 − 600 = 17,800
- Net earnings subject to SE = 17,800 × 92.35% ≈ 16,444 → SE tax ≈ 2,515 → half SE deduction ≈ 1,258
- AGI would be slightly higher than Option A, and your SE tax would be higher than in Option A. So actual method looks better here (mainly because rent is high relative to the simplified rate).

F. Other items & planning tips
- Unreimbursed employee expenses: If that $540 was related to your W-2 job, it is NOT deductible (suspended). If it was business-related for your freelance work, include it on Schedule C.
- Keep records/receipts: Keep the Salvation Army receipt, home-rent/utility records, any invoices or receipts for freelance expenses, and the Nelnet payment records.
- Estimated taxes: Because you have self-employment income, you likely owe SE tax and additional income tax. If you expect similar freelance income in the future, consider making quarterly estimated tax payments or increasing withholding on your W-4 to avoid underpayment penalties.
- QBI deduction: You may qualify for up to 20% of qualified business income from your Schedule C. Tax software or a preparer will compute this; it can reduce taxable income further.
- State tax: Texas has no state income tax, so no state return for wages/income.

G. Next steps / clarifying questions for me
1. Are the $540 “unreimbursed expenses” for your freelance writing (business expenses) or for your W-2 employment? If they are for freelance, include them on Schedule C; if they are employee expenses, they are not deductible.
2. Do you pay utilities, renter’s insurance, or any other housing-related expenses that should be pro‑rated with rent? (That could increase the home-office actual deduction.)
3. Did any of your freelance clients issue 1099‑NEC or 1099‑MISC forms? (You still report all income even if no 1099s were issued.)
4. Did you make any estimated tax payments during the year or have additional credits/deductions (education credits, retirement plan contributions, health insurance self-employed deduction, etc.)?

If you want, I can:
- Draft a checklist of exactly which receipts and forms to gather before preparing the return.
- Run a more precise estimate if you tell me whether the $540 is business-related and whether you have utility/renter-insurance amounts for the home so I can compute the actual home-office allocation and a closer AGI/tax estimate.
- Prepare a step-by-step list of how to fill Schedule C, Form 8829 (if you choose actual method), and Schedule SE for this situation.

Which of those would be most helpful next?
